summary: This informational document, from the Routing Research Group, lists prioritized design goals for a future Internet routing and addressing architecture. It frames challenges in scalability, mobility, multihoming, and inter-domain traffic engineering. It sets goals rather than a solution.

eli5.summary: The internet's address book is getting too big and messy. This is a wish list of what a better system should do before anyone designs it.

questions: design goals for new routing architecture
subtitle: A prioritized list of challenges the Internet routing architecture must address.

tldr.problem: The Internet's routing and addressing system faces critical challenges: the global BGP routing table grows rapidly, networks struggle to support mobility and multi-homing, and renumbering is costly when sites change ISPs.
tldr.mechanism: The Routing Research Group identifies ten design goals for a new routing architecture, ranked by priority, covering scalability, traffic engineering, mobility, security, and deployability.
tldr.outcome: These goals guide the evaluation of candidate routing architectures and help frame the trade-offs any solution must address.

today: RFC 6227 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains a reference for understanding what the Routing Research Group identified as necessary for a scalable Internet routing architecture, even though a complete replacement architecture has not yet been standardized.

sections.title: The Routing Problem
sections.content:
The Internet routing and addressing architecture faces well-recognized challenges. The global BGP routing table is growing rapidly, making the system expensive to operate. Networks that want to stay connected through multiple Internet Service Providers (multi-homing) must announce more address prefixes, which adds to the table. Devices that move between networks (mobility) create dynamic routing updates. Traffic engineering—directing traffic along non-optimal paths for operational reasons—requires injecting more-specific prefixes into the global system. Renumbering a network when changing ISPs is costly and error-prone. A new architecture should address these problems, but nobody yet knows the best way.

The Routing Research Group (RRG) set out to explore an alternate architecture and identify what that new system must achieve. This document presents a prioritized list of design goals to guide that work.
sections.eli5: The internet gets more crowded and complicated every year. This lists the ten things a better system must do.

sections.title: Design Goals and Priorities
sections.content:
The RFC defines ten design goals, each assigned a priority: required (the solution must support this), strongly desired (should support unless impossible or inefficient), or desired (should support). Two goals are required: the new architecture must provide routing security at least as strong as today's system and must be deployable incrementally, continuing to support existing routing functions like policy-based control.

The other eight goals split between strongly desired and desired. Improved routing scalability is strongly desired: the system should scale independently from the growth of the Internet user population. Scalable support for traffic engineering should allow networks to direct traffic without flooding the global routing table. Scalable support for multi-homing should let organizations connect to multiple ISPs without multiplying routing table entries. Simplified renumbering is strongly desired to reduce the cost of site renumbering when changing providers.
sections.eli5: The goals are divided by how important they are. Two must-haves are security and the ability to roll out gradually. Six more are very important. Two are nice to have.

sections.title: Technical Goals for the New Architecture
sections.content:
Decoupling location and identification (desired) addresses a long-standing issue: IP addresses today encode both location information (where in the network a device is) and identification information (what device it is). This overloading limits flexibility. Scalable support for mobility (desired) should allow a device or network to move while maintaining communications, without injecting dynamic updates into the global routing system.

Modularity, composability, and seamlessness (strongly desired) means the new architecture should subdivide into orthogonal subsystems with clean interfaces. If tunneling is used, it should be transparent to endpoints without special workarounds. Routing quality (strongly desired) should match or exceed today's routing in terms of convergence time, stability, and stretch (the ratio of a computed route's length to the shortest possible path).
sections.eli5: The architecture should separate what a device is from where it is. Devices should move without breaking the global system. The system should be modular and clean, and routes should be as short as they are today.

sections.title: Summary of Priorities
sections.content:
The RFC provides a summary table of all ten goals. Two are required: routing security and deployability. Six are strongly desired: scalability, traffic engineering, multi-homing, simplified renumbering, modularity, and routing quality. Two are desired: decoupling location and identification, and mobility. This prioritization reflects the reality that no solution can perfectly optimize all goals at once. The document emphasizes that these are guidelines for design and evaluation, to be applied with good judgment.

The goals were revisited and finalized after the RRG's work on revised routing architectures was complete, so they represent both the starting vision and refinements based on practical experience.
sections.eli5: All ten goals matter, but some are must-haves and others are nice-to-haves. The list helps architects make hard choices when they cannot have everything.
